    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description: Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice.

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to read

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

limit.description: The number of lines to read. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

allow_large.description: Set to true to read a text file, or a line range of one, that is over the usual size limits, up to what still fits in your context. Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

tools.name: ReportFindings
tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

level.description: Effort level the review ran at

findings.description: Verified findings, most-severe first; empty if none survived

file.description: Repo-relative path of the file the finding is in

short_summary.description: Compressed label for compact UI (≤60 chars): the claim alone, no rationale or consequence clause

category.description: Short kebab-case slug of the finding type, e.g. "correctness", "simplification", "efficiency", "test-coverage"

verdict.description: Set when a verify pass ran; absent on inline-only reviews

outcome.description: Set ONLY when re-reporting after applying fixes: what happened to this finding

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: SearchPlugins
tools.description:
Search the user's claude.ai plugin catalog by keyword. Call this when a plugin (slash command, skill bundle, hook, or agent) from the user's org catalog might help complete the task. The user does not need to name a plugin: search when the task depends on their team's own process, systems or data and nothing you already have, the project's own scripts included, covers it.

Examples:
- "use the deploy plugin" → keywords ["deploy"]
- "is there something for linting?" → keywords ["lint", "format", "code quality"]
- "ship this to staging" → keywords ["deploy", "release", "staging"]
- "review this contract against our playbook" → keywords ["legal", "contract", "playbook"]
- "which deals close this week?" → keywords ["sales", "pipeline", "crm"]

Do not search unasked for one-off questions or tasks you can handle directly ("explain this regex", "fix this typo"), or after the user ignored a suggestion in this conversation.

Returns a ranked list with id, name, description, and whether the plugin is already enabled for this session (in a channel session, whether the channel has it). When results fit and SuggestPluginInstall is among your tools, call it to render the install card; otherwise relay the relevant results in text instead. If nothing relevant, proceed without mentioning that you searched.

keywords.description: Keyword phrases describing the user's intent.

tools.name: SendUserFile
tools.description:
Send files to the user. Use this for any file the user would want to see — a generated diagram, a report, a screenshot, a built artifact — and you want it surfaced, not just mentioned. Send deliverables as they are produced, not batched at the end of the task: a complete draft or a meaningfully updated version of the thing the user asked for is worth sending mid-task, so they can follow progress and redirect early. Do NOT send routine working files — scratch files, debug output, partial fragments, or every incremental save of something you're still actively editing; each call renders a file card in the conversation, and a stream of cards for one file is noise. Re-send a file only when it has meaningfully changed since the last send. Paths can be absolute or relative to the current working directory.

Add a `caption` when a one-liner of context helps ("the failing case is row 42", "before vs after"). Skip it if the file speaks for itself.

Set `status` on every call. Use `proactive` when you're initiating — the user is away and you want this to reach their phone (build artifact ready, report generated). Use `normal` when replying to something the user just said.

Set `display` to choose how the file is presented. Use `'render'` when the user should see the content inline in the side panel right now — a chart, a rendered HTML page, a diagram, an image. Use `'attach'` when the file is something they'll save and open elsewhere — source code, a spreadsheet, a document for another app — and an inline preview would just be noise. Leave it unset to let the client decide by file type.

Files must already exist on the local filesystem — the tool sends files, it doesn't fetch URLs or render content. When unsure of a path, verify with ls first; absolute paths avoid ambiguity about the working directory.

Example: SendUserFile({ files: ["report.md"], caption: "Here's the report.", status: "normal" })

files.description: File paths (absolute or relative to cwd) to send to the user. Always pass an array, even for a single file.

caption.description: Optional short caption for the file(s).

status.description: Use 'proactive' when you're surfacing a file the user hasn't asked for and needs to see now — a generated artifact, a completed report. Use 'normal' when replying to something the user just said.

display.description: How the client should present the file. 'render' opens it inline in the side panel (for HTML, SVG, Mermaid, images, PDFs — anything the user wants to look at now). 'attach' shows a download card only, no inline preview (for deliverables the user will save and open elsewhere). Omit to let the client decide by file type — today that means renderable types render and everything else attaches, same as before this parameter existed.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: SuggestPluginInstall
tools.description:
Render an inline card of plugins the user can add to claude.ai, taken from SearchPlugins results. The card handles all install UI; do not describe the plugins in text.

Offer one when the task is the kind a plugin could take over or make repeatable (deploys, reviews against a team process, or the ticket, data and document workflows a user's org may have packaged as plugins) and nothing enabled covers it; the user does not need to ask about plugins. Also when they ask for plugin recommendations. First call SearchPlugins with keywords drawn from the task, then pass the relevant results here: pluginId from each result's id, pluginName from its name, description as returned. Set trigger ('proactive' when you initiated this from task context, 'user_asked' when they asked). Use ListPlugins for plugins they already have.

After the card, continue the task. Example: "ship this to staging" and a deploy plugin that is not enabled → contextLabel "For your deploys".

Do NOT call this for one-off questions you can answer directly, when you are unsure a plugin would help, when SearchPlugins returned nothing relevant (then continue the task without mentioning the search), or if you already rendered a plugin or skill suggestion this conversation and the user didn't engage.

contextLabel.description: Short header tying the suggestion to the user request.

tools.name: SuggestSkills
tools.description:
Render a card of standalone skills the user can add — org, shared, or Anthropic skills not yet enabled.

Call this when the task is one a skill could make repeatable — drafting in a house style, reviews against a playbook, a recurring workflow — and nothing enabled covers it; the user does not need to ask about skills. Also when they ask for recommendations, or when ListSkills returned zero matches. Use ListSkills for skills they already have.

Do NOT call this for one-off questions you can answer directly, when you are unsure a skill would help, or if you already rendered a suggestion this conversation and the user didn't engage.

Pass keywords drawn from the task itself, and set trigger ('proactive' when you initiated this from task context, 'user_asked' when they asked). If the result is empty and the trigger was proactive, continue the task without mentioning that you searched; if the user asked, tell them you found nothing new to add.

keywords.description: Topic keywords from the user's request.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: WebFetch
tools.description:
Fetches a URL, converts the page to markdown, and answers `prompt` against it using a small fast model.

- Fails on authenticated/private URLs — use an authenticated MCP tool or `gh` for those instead. claude.ai artifact links (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}) are published artifacts: read them with the Artifact tool (action "read"), not WebFetch or curl.
- Fails on localhost and other hostnames without a dot; for a local server, use curl via Bash.
- HTTP is upgraded to HTTPS. Cross-host redirects are returned to you rather than followed; call again with the redirect URL.
- Responses are cached for 15 minutes per URL.

url.description: The URL to fetch content from

prompt.description: The prompt to run on the fetched content

offset.description: Character position in the page text to start reading from. Use it to read on through a page too long for one call, with the value the previous result gave.

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to write (must be absolute, not relative)

content.description: The content to write to the file

tools.name: mcp__1a59c906-04da-521d-bda7-7f71b9f9e01c__batch
tools.description: Create a doc, or apply several operations to one doc atomically.

tools.name: mcp__1a59c906-04da-521d-bda7-7f71b9f9e01c__guide
tools.description: Docs guides: topic.instructions repeats the server instructions. Read it only if your client dropped them. Also topic.<name>, refusal.<code>. After a doc's birth → ["topic.index"].

items.description: topic.<name> (instructions, index, editing, tabs, comments, charts, chart-definition, diagram, uploads, sharing, skill) or refusal.<code>; several per call is fine.

tools.name: mcp__1a59c906-04da-521d-bda7-7f71b9f9e01c__update
tools.description: Edit a tab's contents, rename a doc or tab, or change a stored value.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a proposal you made with start_session (initiation "own_initiative" or "offer") that the user has not started.

Call this when it went stale: the work was done here after all (by you or the user), it turned out unnecessary, or you proposed a better-scoped replacement (propose the new one first, then dismiss the old task_id). A card the user answered has already left, "Do it here" included, so it needs no call.

task_id.description: The task_id the start_session proposal returned.

reason.description: Optional one-line reason the suggestion is no longer needed, e.g. "fixed in this session" or "superseded by task_ab12cd34".

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__hand_off_to_session
tools.description: Move the task you are in the middle of into its own session (a fork of this conversation plus your remaining plan) so you can answer the user now. Use it when a new user message about something else arrives mid-task — not for small corrections or when the user said to keep the work here. In a worktree the fork gets a fresh worktree, normally cut from your branch tip: commit first (uncommitted edits stay here). Bold title line and one sentence right before the call; after it, stop that task here and answer the new message — no recap.

title.description: Under 60 chars; names the task being moved.

remaining_plan.description: What is left to do: steps, files, what done looks like.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

title.description: Short noun-phrase title for the chapter (under 40 chars). Shown in the table of contents.

summary.description: Optional one-line summary of what this chapter covers. Shown on hover in the table of contents.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__read_widget_context
tools.description: Read context from an embedded interactive widget. Widgets are rendered alongside chat from prior tool calls and can be interacted with by the user. Call this when you need to know the current state of a widget.

tool_name.description: The name of the widget tool to get context for

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

scope.description: Required with items: "first_task", "continuation" or "new_task" (see the tool description). Omit on advance / done / start updates.

session.description: When you delegated this step to a session you started: that session's short name (from start_session's result). The app shows its live state on the step.

items.description: The whole plan, in order (1–12 steps); replaces the previous list.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields — recap and ask are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label is the user's words back to you:
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

recap.description: Two or three short sentences to the user (≤300 chars): what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified. Its first sentence is the sidebar status. It must stand on its own, since it is also read away from the transcript and the box draws under anything you write after this call: never point at anything else in the conversation ("listed below", "see above", "in my message").

ask.description: The one question (≤100 chars) when the next move is the user's call — a choice, a go-ahead (to act here on what this turn found, say), an approval: the decision alone, with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give (actions[0] is your pick). Like the recap, never point at anything else in the conversation. Omit it, and actions, when nothing waits on the user.

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available now, or one your own work this turn made available; anything else is refused, and one that stops being available later is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and the other answers), so do not guess. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Fix 2 instead", "Not now": a button, not a sentence. A click sends it to you as the user's answer. No leading / or !. Ignored for an app action (the app's own label is used).

actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. They are answers to your ask: the first accepts your recommendation, and another is there only when it is a realistic alternative the user might pick instead — not a menu of everything you mentioned. When blocked is true, they are the most likely answers to your question. While Auto-fix is on for the session's PR, none offers to watch it, fix CI, resolve conflicts or address comments.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

name.description: Tool name (e.g. computer, navigate, find, form_input, read_page). browser_batch cannot be nested. A tabs_create's new tabId is only returned when the batch ends — load that tab in a later call.

input.description: That tool's input — same shape you'd pass when calling it directly. For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

actions.description: List of tool calls to execute sequentially. Example: [{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"left_click","ref":"ref_12"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"type","text":"hello"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"screenshot"}}]

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__find
tools.description: Search the current page in the Browser pane for elements whose accessibility-tree line (role / name / text) contains `query`, case-insensitively. Returns up to 20 `ref_N` matches usable with `computer`/`form_input`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

query.description: Text to look for in an element's role, name or text (case-insensitive substring, e.g. "Sign in", "search", "Add to cart").

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__form_input
tools.description: Set the value of a form element identified by `ref` (from read_page/find). Handles input/textarea/select/checkbox/contenteditable.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

ref.description: Element reference ID from the read_page tool (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2")

content.content:
**What it checks:** Whether each citation in an LLM's answer is accurate. It flags quotes missing from the source, and claims that the quoted section contradicts or doesn't address. Each citation gets one of four verdicts: verified, unsupported, contradicted, or fabricated.

**Inputs:** Yes, it needs the source document (here, RFC 7519) and the citations, each with a claim, an optional quote, and a section number. The model judges only the section text you supply, so it needs that evidence provided.

**Primitives:**
- **String match:** Normalizes whitespace and quote characters, then checks whether the quote appears verbatim. A quote that fails is marked fabricated without calling the model.
- **`Choice` question:** Asks how the section relates to the claim (supports, contradicts, or says nothing). The highest-probability option sets the verdict.
- **Confidence threshold:** Verdicts at or above 0.8 are accepted automatically. Lower-confidence verdicts go to a human.

**World knowledge:** No. The page describes the model as judging the claim against the supplied section only.

**Accuracy (8 citations, `jev-1.12`, 2026-08-16):**
- The four accurate citations were all verified, at confidence 0.93 to 0.99.
- The four planted failures were all flagged: one fabricated (string match), one contradicted (0.99), and two unsupported (0.27 and 0.56), both sent to review.
- This is a small test set, so these numbers don't establish general accuracy.

**Cost and latency:** The code records per-call seconds and token counts, but the page doesn't report those figures.

## Pricing, cost, and latency

The index has no dedicated pricing, cost, or latency page. The closest material:

- **Parallel questions** cookbook: batching a 13-question briefing into one call is "12.2x cheaper and 10.0x faster with no change in answers."
- **Models**: listed with no description.
- **Request rules and errors**: request limits, compression, and HTTP status codes.
- **Answers and responses** (Python SDK) and **Usage** (JavaScript SDK): token usage in responses.

## Citation check and claim verification

- **Double-checking citations**: catches wrong or hallucinated citations by checking against the source document. One Choice question decides whether the quote's context supports the claim.

No standalone claim verification page exists.

## Cookbooks for triage before an expensive step

- **SDE cascade**: a cheap model extracts structured data, TypeSafe checks each field, and a reasoning model is called only when a check fires. This is the closest match.
- **Guardrails for LLMs**: screens each message and passes, reviews, blocks, or escalates it based on thresholds you set.
- **Classifying RAG passages**: scores retrieved passages so only relevant ones reach the answering model.
- **Self-consistency: nouls** and **Self-consistency: choices**: route uncertain results to human review.
- **Date extraction**: uses confidence-based review on extracted dates.

Related patterns: **Confidence-gated routing** and **Intent routing** (deterministic logic, a specialist LLM, or a human).

content.text:
Yes, but probably not where you'd expect.

**What TypeSafe can't do:** search the web. Searches are now 87% of the bill, so swapping in TypeSafe for any single step won't make that cost go away. It only saves money if it means we **search fewer claims**.

**Where it could help, biggest win first:**

1. **A filter before searching.** For each claim, TypeSafe answers a quick question like "would a careful viewer doubt this or want it checked?" and returns a probability. Only claims above a cutoff get searched. These judgments are fast, about 150ms each according to your `RESEARCH.md`, so they suit live use. In our test this would matter a lot: on Kurzgesagt, all 10 claims came back supported, so ideally most of them would never have been searched. On the seed-oil video, most claims would still go through, which is what you want.
   - **The catch:** TypeSafe is built to judge text you give it, not to know facts on its own. It's good at telling "a health claim with a suspicious exact number" from "a rounded textbook date." It shouldn't be trusted to decide what's actually false. That's still the search step's job.
2. **Finding claims in the captions.** `RESEARCH.md` already planned this: one judgment per caption sentence asking "is this a checkable factual claim?", replacing Haiku's claim-finding call. It saves only a little money because that step is cheap, but it's faster.
3. **Judging the search results.** TypeSafe's citation-check example does exactly this: given a source, does it support, contradict, or not address the claim? This only replaces model token cost, which is now 13% of the bill. Not worth it for cost alone.

**Two things I don't know:**
- TypeSafe's per-call price. Its docs don't list one, so check your TypeSafe account. If it costs more than about 1¢ a claim, the filter saves nothing.
- Whether the filter would let a false claim slip through. That's the real risk. We can measure it for almost nothing on the 30 claims we already graded: the filter has to keep every claim that came back contradicted or misleading, and drop as many of the supported ones as it can.

**My recommendation:** run that filter test next. It's a short script, and you already have a TypeSafe key in `.env`. Before I build it, what result would make it worth keeping? My suggestion: it keeps all 8 of the claims the tuned run flagged and skips at least half of the rest.

input.recap: TypeSafe can't replace web search, which is now 87% of the cost, but it could filter out claims before they get searched. Whether that filter misses false claims, and what TypeSafe charges per call, are still unknown.

content.content:
## Score question shape

A Score request has `state`, `model`, and `questions`. Each Score question is an object with `type`, `instructions`, and `criteria`:

```json
{
  "state": "The export button crashes the settings page in Safari. It works in Chrome, but a few of our customers only use Safari.",
  "model": "jev-1.13.0",
  "questions": {
    "bug_severity": {
      "type": "score",
      "instructions": "How severe is the reported issue?",
      "criteria": [
        "Cosmetic; no impact to functionality",
        "Broken or degraded feature, but workaround exists",
        "Blocking issue; no workaround exists"
      ]
    }
  }
}
```

- `type` is always `"score"`.
- `instructions` is the question the model answers.
- `criteria` is an ordered array of level descriptions, from low to high. It needs at least two levels and accepts up to 10.
- The key `bug_severity` is your question ID. The model doesn't see it, and the answer returns under the same ID.

## How the answer is returned

The response has one entry in `answers` for each question ID:

```json
{
  "model": "jev-1.13.0",
  "answers": {
    "bug_severity": {
      "type": "score",
      "score": 1.43,
      "confidence": 0.35,
      "legend": {
        "0": "Cosmetic; no impact to functionality",
        "1": "Broken or degraded feature, but workaround exists",
```

Bar set before running: keep all 8 claims the tuned Haiku run didn't call

  high (Pope Leo's ballot: 0.96), because it can't know recent events, so news
  videos would get no savings at all.
- About 560 input tokens per claim. TypeSafe's price per token isn't in its
  docs, so the cost of the filter itself is unknown.
EOF

content.text: Plan updated: step 4 of 4 is in progress.
Shown in the next-step box. Your closing message is your answer to the user: write it now, in full, as the last thing you say this turn. The box asks your question, so do not ask it again.

**The filter didn't pass.** It's good at spotting claims that *sound* suspicious, but it can't tell which ones are actually wrong, so it saves very little.

**The bar we set:** keep all 8 claims that Haiku flagged, and skip at least half of the 22 that came back fine.

| Cutoff | Flagged claims kept | Fine claims skipped | Search saving |
|---|---|---|---|
| Lenient (keeps all 8) | 8 of 8 ✅ | 5 of 22 ❌ | ~15% |
| Stricter | 7 of 8 | 10 of 22 | ~35% |
| Strict | 5 of 8 ❌ | 16 of 22 | ~60% |

**Why it falls short:**
- 🟢 **It ranks the scary stuff well.** "One serving is toxic for 3 years" came out at the top; textbook dates like the Holocene came out at the bottom.
- 🔴 **It can't know recent news.** Every PBS claim scored as doubtful, even true ones like "Pope Leo mailed his ballot" (0.96, the second most suspicious claim of all 30). On a news video, it would skip nothing.
- The one flagged claim it scored low is the Göbekli Tepe claim we couldn't grade anyway, because the captions misheard the name. Leaving that one out, the stricter cutoff almost reaches the bar (skips 10 of 22) but still falls just short.

**Bottom line:** at best it saves about 2–3¢ on a 17¢ video, and we don't know what TypeSafe itself charges for the roughly 560 input tokens per claim. That doesn't seem worth the risk of skipping a claim that should have been checked. I'd keep TypeSafe for the job `RESEARCH.md` planned for it: picking out checkable sentences in the captions live, where its speed matters. The search step stays as it is, and live verdicts on the tuned Haiku come to about 17¢ a video.

The full ranking is in [filter.md](eval/results/filter.md). Your call on the 1865 seed-oil verdict is still open, but it doesn't block the commit; I can record whatever you decide afterward.

content.text:
**The claim** (from the seed-oil video): "Seed oils were developed around 1865 and weren't originally intended for human consumption."

**The tuned Haiku said "supported."** Its own explanation, though, says this is only true of cottonseed oil: other seed oils have different histories.

**Opus said "misleading,"** for the same reason, and because cottonseed oil was turned into food fairly soon after.

**The question:** would you, as a viewer, want that claim flagged as misleading, or is "supported" fine? If you say "misleading," Haiku's count goes to 1 wrong verdict, the same as Opus. If you say "supported," it gets none wrong.

## Decisions

- **2026-11-02 — Live verdicts for red flags only.** Dylan wants a verdict to
  appear when the claim is spoken. Claude's concern: if every supported claim
  pops up, people learn to ignore them. Agreed: only contradicted or misleading
  claims appear live (a small chip by the controls for a few seconds, click for
  details); supported ones stay in the list and the count. Claims are checked
  in time order a few minutes ahead of the playhead, so verdicts are ready in
  time and nothing past where the viewer stops gets paid for.
- **2026-11-02 — Test verdict quality before building the interface.** Claude
  suggested it (the biggest unknown is whether verdicts are any good); Dylan
  agreed and asked for health-influencer and news videos besides Kurzgesagt,
  since a Kurzgesagt video is a good answer key but not one people doubt. A
  toggle that's always visible and says "Nothing to check" was Dylan's call,
  over hiding it on videos with no claims.
- **2026-11-02 — YouTube first, any topic, desktop.** Dylan wants to focus on
  desktop, where YouTube is far more practical than TikTok. A share-to-Discord
  bot was considered and dropped: Dylan pointed out people could just share a
  link with their own AI app. A universal checker that reads the whole screen
  automatically was Dylan's idea; Claude raised privacy, cost, and noise, so it
  becomes a later hotkey checker sharing the same server. Dylan chose any topic
  over one area (health, money, science) because it's more appealing.
- **2026-11-01 — Back to the fact-checker.** Dylan switched back because it's
  the more interesting project. The reason for shelving it on 2026-10-19
  (browser extensions aren't one of the listed platforms) is resolved: course
  staff said an extension is OK. The schoolwork assistant built in between
  (screenshot and Canvas import, What now?, History, Overview) is saved at the
  `schoolwork-assistant` tag, with its own PLAN.md there; its unfinished new
  look was never tried by Dylan.
- **2026-10-12 — Idea: fact-checker for short-form video.** Dylan's own idea,
  chosen over suggestions (scam shield, section-swap market, others) that didn't
  interest Dylan. Plain written-claim fact-checking already exists (Google's
  tool), so the value is in checking video as you watch it.
- **2026-10-12 — Chrome extension, not a paste-a-link web app.** Dylan found
  pasting links "too useless"; the point is to be active while watching.
- **2026-10-12 — TikTok first, Instagram deferred.** TikTok's page includes
  caption tracks (including auto-generated ones). Instagram has no public
  transcript, and the only route goes against its terms of service.
- **2026-10-12 — Check anything checkable**, not one topic.
- **2026-10-12 — TypeSafe for judgments.** Fast, parallel typed judgments per
  sentence fit the "is this a checkable claim?" filter.
- **2026-10-12 — Mobile: Android later, iOS out.** iOS doesn't let apps read
  other apps' screens. Android can (screen capture plus on-device OCR, or a
  share-sheet target). The extension comes first because debugging the
  judging is easier there; Android reuses the same server endpoint.
- **2026-10-12 — Smaller UI.** Dylan felt the first mockup took too much space
  and would hurt the viewing experience. Iterated: corner dot, then a button
  in TikTok's side buttons, then (because TikTok's layout could change and
  break it) a button anchored to the video element itself. Pausing while
  reading was Dylan's pick from the suggestions.
- **2026-10-12 — AI detection as signals, not a detector.** Frame-analysis
  detectors don't publish false-positive rates and do badly on real footage
  with fast cuts. Use TikTok's label, caption and hashtags, and comments
  instead. See `RESEARCH.md`.

- **2026-10-12 — TikTok is the goal; expand afterwards.** Android moved from
  committed goal to stretch, given 24 hours and six milestones.
- **2026-10-12 — Add a small language model alongside TypeSafe.** TypeSafe
  judges and selects but doesn't write text; rewriting messy caption claims
  into searchable form needs a language model. Dylan sees combining the two as

Before I build, let's agree on what done looks like, because this is a big feature. The extension still only reads TikTok, and there's no server yet. Live verdicts need three new pieces:

1. **A YouTube caption reader.** It replaces the TikTok one; the caption parsing carries over.
2. **A small server on your laptop.** It holds the Anthropic key, finds the claims, and checks them in time order a few minutes ahead of where you're watching. API keys can't go inside the extension, because anyone who installs it could read them.
3. **The red-flag chip by the video controls,** plus the toggle with the claim count.

**Proposed finish line.** You run the server, open the seed-oil video in Chrome, and press play:
- The toggle by the controls says "Finding claims…", then "10 claims".
- Around **4:03**, a red chip appears: *"Contradicted: one serving toxic for 3 years"*. It stays a few seconds, then fades.
- Clicking the chip pauses the video and shows the explanation and sources beside it, never over it.
- On the **Kurzgesagt** video, no chips appear at all.

**One choice I'm making that you can overrule:** the server runs on your laptop, not online. That means classmates try it on your laptop for now. Putting it online so anyone can install the extension comes later.

This will probably take more than one session. The first one should get as far as the claim count showing on a real YouTube video.

content.text:
There is evidence, and it mostly backs your instinct rather than my original plan.

**The research that supports you: the "implied truth effect"** (Pennycook and colleagues, 2020). When only some false headlines carry a warning, people rate the *unlabeled* headlines as more accurate, including false ones that simply hadn't been checked. Silence reads as "this is true." For your app, that means a claim with no chip looks validated, even if it hasn't been checked yet or the check failed. As I recall, the same study found that labeling some true headlines as verified largely removed the effect. I'm fairly confident of that finding, but I'm working from memory rather than checking the paper.

**The research behind my concern: warning fatigue.** Studies of security warnings show people stop noticing alerts that appear too often. That's real, but it's about alerts that interrupt you. A small, quiet confirmation isn't the same thing.

**What both point to:** show every verdict, but don't give them equal weight.
- 🔴 **Contradicted or misleading:** the red chip as planned, noticeable, click for details.
- 🟢 **Supported:** a small, quiet check mark that shows briefly at the claim's time. It doesn't pop or grab attention, but you can click it for sources.
- ⚪ **Unverified or not checked yet:** shown as its own state, so "no mark" never gets mistaken for "true."

The Kurzgesagt part of the finish line would become: **small green checks appear as claims are spoken, and no red chips.** The seed-oil video gets red chips around 4:03, plus green checks on the claims that held up, like hexane being used in processing.

Does that version of the finish line work for you?

1. **Current milestone: claims from a YouTube video.** A toggle beside the

   "Nothing to check", "No captions", or "Couldn't check: retry". Clicking it

   Then try cheaper models on the same three videos. The TikTok reader (`src/tiktok.ts`) is replaced by a YouTube one;
   the caption parsing and extension plumbing carry over.
2. On-demand checking: Google Fact Check Tools API, then web evidence, then
   per-source supports/contradicts judgments.
3. Hotkey checker: press a key (or drag a box) to check the claims in whatever
   is on screen, through the same server.
4. AI signals and an audio fallback for videos without captions, if still
   wanted.

**Reminder for Claude:** once on-demand checking works end to end, remind Dylan
to build the test set (20-30 videos with known answers) and measure accuracy
per topic before tuning anything. Kurzgesagt publishes a sources document for
each video, which makes its videos a ready-made answer key. Dylan asked for this
reminder on 2026-10-12.

## Done (unverified until Dylan reviews)

- 2026-10-12: Promo trailer (`promo/`), 36 s at 1080p with a synthesized
  soundtrack. Shows the planned design, labeled "Concept preview."

## Decisions
## Problems

- **2026-11-02 — YouTube guards its captions.** Fetching a video's caption
  file or transcript from outside the page returns nothing (it needs a token
  the player adds). Inside the page it works: the player's own caption request
  carries the token, and so does YouTube's "Show transcript" panel. The
  extension will read captions from inside the page.
- **2026-11-02 — Verdicts from memory.** With 12 checks at once, about a third
  of web searches failed and the model answered from memory; those were the
  wrong verdicts. The script now runs two at a time, retries, and reports
  failed searches. Rule for the app: no source, no verdict.
- **2026-10-12 — Couldn't confirm caption field names.** Both videos inspected
  live were music-only, and then TikTok showed a CAPTCHA, which Claude does not
  solve. Caption parsing uses field names from earlier TikTok pages and accepts
  both known spellings; Dylan's first live test confirms them.
- **2026-10-12 — Trailer render failed on this laptop.** Windows blocks some
  unsigned programs (Smart App Control): Remotion's downloaded headless Chrome
  and its `ffprobe.exe` were refused, while `ffmpeg.exe` was allowed. Fixes:
  `promo/remotion.config.ts` renders with the installed (signed) Chrome, and
  the soundtrack is added with ffmpeg after rendering so ffprobe is never
  needed. Also, TypeScript 7 lacks the API Remotion uses to read tsconfig
  (JSX broke), so `promo/` pins TypeScript 5.

# Built-in browser

The built-in browser is a real browser pane inside the Claude desktop app, separate from the person's Chrome. Its tools are named `mcp__Claude_Browser__*` when the session itself runs inside the desktop app, and `mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__*` when the session runs in the cloud (started from the web, a phone, or the desktop app) and is linked to the person's computer. The names after the prefix are the same either way, Claude uses whichever prefix is actually present, and this skill refers to the tools by the part after the prefix.

If the only built-in browser tool present is `enable__mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser`, Claude calls it first: it turns the built-in browser on for this conversation, and the `mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__*` tools appear once it has run.

## What the person can see

The browser pane shares the desktop app's side panel with artifacts, documents, and file previews, and the panel shows one of them at a time. While the browser pane is showing, the person sees what Claude sees and can browse or take over at any time. While something else is open in the panel, or the panel is closed, the built-in browser keeps working but the person cannot see it.

Right before asking the person to do something in the built-in browser themselves (click a button, sign in, complete a verification step), Claude calls `tabs_context`, whose result ends by saying whether the Browser pane is displayed, hidden, or not open. If the pane is not open, Claude opens the page first and checks again. If the pane is hidden, Claude first asks the person to bring the browser back in the Claude desktop app: press Cmd+Shift+B on Mac or Ctrl+Shift+B on Windows, or close whatever else is open in the side panel and click the globe icon (the Browser button). Claude then says what to do in the browser. Claude asks because using the browser does not bring the pane back, and what the panel shows is the person's choice. Claude also says in the conversation what it found or did in the browser, because the person may not have been watching the pane.

## Sign-ins persist, and they are the person's

The built-in browser keeps its own persistent profile, shared across the desktop app's sessions. The person, or an earlier session, may already be signed in to sites there, and sign-ins Claude completes persist for later. Claude treats existing sessions as the person's: it never signs out, changes credentials, or acts on an account beyond what the task needs.

## Tabs

The built-in browser has tabs. `preview_start` with a `url` opens an additional tab at that URL in one call and returns a `tabId`, leaving existing tabs untouched, so Claude prefers it over `tabs_create` followed by `navigate` when the destination is already known. `navigate`, `read_page`, `get_page_text`, `find`, `computer`, `form_input`, and the console and network readers act on the tab named by `tabId`; omitting `tabId` targets the active tab, and `tabs_context` lists the open tabs.

## Loading via ToolSearch

Claude loads the built-in browser tools in bulk, not one-by-one: if they are in the deferred list, Claude loads them all in a single ToolSearch call whose query is their full name prefix, for example `{ query: "mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__", max_results: 64 }`.

## Reading pages

Claude prefers `get_page_text` and `read_page` over screenshots for reading, because they return the page's actual text and structure rather than pixels of the visible viewport. `computer` with action "screenshot" is for when the visual layout is the point or the person asks to see the page.

## Site approvals, blocked sites, and request_access

Depending on the person's approval settings, the person may be asked to approve a site before Claude acts on it, and some sites are blocked outright. Claude waits for a pending approval rather than working around it. If a page is refused or an approval is declined, Claude tells the person and moves on rather than retrying.

When the tools carry the `mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__` prefix, approvals can be answered from any of the person's devices and may take a moment to arrive, and the session may also have a `request_access` tool. If a browser tool answers that the site is not allowed yet and `request_access` is present, Claude calls it with that site's URL and scope "once" (or "site" when the task will keep using that site), waits for the person's answer, and then retries the original tool. Without `request_access`, a refused site is handled as above: Claude tells the person and moves on.

## What the built-in browser cannot open

The built-in browser cannot open `file://` URLs or `localhost` servers that Claude starts itself, because those run where Claude's shell runs, which is not where the browser pane runs. To show the person HTML that Claude generated, Claude uses an artifact instead.

## When the built-in browser cannot be reached

When the tools carry the `mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__` prefix, the pane runs in the Claude desktop app on the person's computer while Claude runs elsewhere, so it is reachable only while that app is open and online. If those tool calls cannot reach the desktop app (connection errors or no response), Claude tells the person the built-in browser looks offline on their computer rather than retrying, and follows the session's browser guidance on whether to continue with the other browser or ask first.

# Video Fact Check

A Chrome extension that watches TikTok alongside you: it finds checkable claims
in what a video says, checks them against sources when you ask, and reports
signs a video is AI-generated. See `PLAN.md` for where the project stands and
`RESEARCH.md` for why it is built this way.

Current state (milestone 1): when a TikTok video starts playing, the extension
prints its transcript and TikTok's AI label to the browser console.

## Requirements

- [Node.js](https://nodejs.org/) 24 or newer (the tests run TypeScript directly)
- Google Chrome

## Build

```bash
npm install
npm run build
```

The built scripts land in `extension/dist/`. Use `npm run watch` to rebuild on
every save.

## Load it in Chrome

1. Open `chrome://extensions`.
2. Turn on **Developer mode** (top right).
3. Click **Load unpacked** and choose this project's `extension` folder.
4. After rebuilding, click the reload arrow on the extension's card, then
   reload the TikTok tab.

## Try it

1. Open [tiktok.com](https://www.tiktok.com) and play a video.
2. Open DevTools (F12) and go to the **Console** tab.
3. Type `[Fact check]` into the console's filter box.

Each video you watch prints once, with its AI label, caption, on-screen text,
and transcript.

## Develop

```bash
npm test           # unit tests
npm run typecheck  # TypeScript checks
npm run format     # format with Prettier
```

All code that depends on how TikTok's site is built lives in `src/tiktok.ts`.
When TikTok changes its site, start there.

## Promo trailer

`promo/` holds a 36-second trailer made with [Remotion](https://www.remotion.dev/)
(videos written as React code). It shows the planned design and is labeled
"Concept preview" until those features exist. It has its own dependencies:

```bash
cd promo
npm install
npm run studio   # live preview with sound in the browser
npm run render   # writes out/trailer.mp4 (1080p, with soundtrack)
npm run poster   # writes out/poster.png
```

The script and timing live in `promo/src/timeline.ts`; the soundtrack is
synthesized by `promo/scripts/soundtrack.ts` from the same timeline, so sound
effects stay in sync when timing changes. Rendering needs Google Chrome
installed (see `promo/remotion.config.ts`).

## Accuracy check

`eval/check.ts` finds the checkable claims in a saved transcript and checks
each one with Claude and web search, writing a report to `eval/results/`. It
needs `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` in `.env` and costs about $1.25 per video.

```bash
npm run check-claims -- eval/transcripts/<name>.txt
```

Transcripts are kept out of Git; results and grades are in `eval/RESULTS.md`.

- [Hexane - an overview (ScienceDirect)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/neuroscience/hexane): Describes hexane as a minor component of gasoline and states it is used as a solvent in extracting soybean, cottonseed, flaxseed, and other oil seeds.

- [Is hexane in food a cause for concern? (EUFIC)](https://www.eufic.org/en/misinformation/article/is-hexane-in-food-a-cause-for-concern): States hexane is a petroleum-derived solvent widely used to extract oils from seeds such as soybeans, rapeseed, and sunflower, and that refining removes almost all of it from the final oil.
## [1:30] MISLEADING: Americans get about 25 to 30% of their calories from seed oils.

- [Abstract P135: Dietary Sources Of Linoleic Acid (LA) Differ By Race/ethnicity In Adults (NHANES 2015-2016)](https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/circ.143.suppl_1.P135): Reports that across the adult population, 7.14% of overall caloric intake was attributable to linoleic acid.

- [Seed Oils, Inflammation, and Calories: What the Data Shows](https://nutrola.app/en/blog/seed-oils-inflammation-and-calories-what-data-actually-shows): Says estimates put added fats and oils (including butter and other fats, not only seed oils) at about 20-25% of energy in the average American diet, a broader category than seed oils alone.
## [2:32] CONTRADICTED: Fast food restaurants reuse their frying oil around a hundred times.

- [Cooking Oil is Expensive. How Many Times Can You Safely Reuse It? - Rebirth Biofuels](https://rebirthbiofuels.com/blog/reuse-cooking-oil/): Typically frying oil can be reused 8 to 10 times, and many fast food restaurants filter daily and replace oil with new oil once a week.

- [Can You Reuse Frying Oil? - WebstaurantStore](https://www.webstaurantstore.com/blog/5336/can-you-reuse-frying-oil.html): Most restaurants reuse frying oil 3–5 times, and fryer oil should be changed once or twice a week on average.
## [3:02] SUPPORTED: The process for producing seed oils was developed around 1865, and the oils were not originally intended for human consumption.

- [The Shocking Origin of Vegetable Oil — Garbage!](https://fung.substack.com/p/the-shocking-origin-of-vegetable): Says commercial production became possible in the 1850s as technology matured, and that cottonseed oil was initially a worthless byproduct before being marketed as food.

- [Dr. Otto's Amazing Oil (Penn State)](https://pabook.libraries.psu.edu/literary-cultural-heritage-map-pa/feature-articles/dr-ottos-amazing-oil): Notes that early cottonseed oil was dark and that food-grade oil development was slow at first, picking up later.
## [4:03] CONTRADICTED: The oxidative stress from smoking persists for about 6 months to a year after quitting.

- [Persistence of oxidant and protease burden in the airways after smoking cessation](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2697135/): Levels of several oxidative stress markers in induced sputum were very similar in never smokers and healthy ex-smokers who quit more than 20 years earlier, suggesting oxidative stress declines over time after quitting.

- [Reduction in oxidatively generated DNA damage following smoking cessation - PMC](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3104490): Smoking cessation reduced specific oxidative DNA damage markers by roughly 30-50 percent within about 11 weeks, in a small study of 19 participants.
## [4:03] CONTRADICTED: A single serving of seed oil has toxic effects in the body for about three years.

- [Concerns about the health effects of industrially produced seed oils are without scientific foundation: a scoping narrative review of the clinical and observational evidence](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/10408398.2026.2657527): The overall balance of RCT, observational, and Mendelian randomization evidence does not support claims of harm from seed oil intake or linoleic acid exposure.

- [Are Seed Oils Really Toxic?](https://guthealthnerd.substack.com/p/are-seed-oils-really-toxic): States that the claim that everyday seed oil use causes inflammation isn't backed up by good trials, and that oil reheated repeatedly breaks down, which is a real concern.
## [4:34] CONTRADICTED: Seed oils damage mitochondria and cause insulin resistance, leading to fatty liver, obesity, heart disease and increased cancer risk.

- [Seed Oils and Blood Sugar: What the Controversy Is Really About](https://www.healthspectra.com/seed-oils-and-blood-sugar-what-the-controversy-is-really-about/): Cites a Diabetes Care meta-analysis of 20 cohort studies finding higher linoleic acid levels linked to lower type 2 diabetes risk, and notes theoretical oxidized-LA mechanisms lack direct human evidence.

- [Linoleic Acid: A Narrative Review of the Effects of Increased Intake in the Standard American Diet and Associations with Chronic Disease](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10386285/): Advocates the mitochondrial and oxidized-LA hypothesis, citing mostly animal and mechanistic studies, which supports the claim's mechanism only as a hypothesis.
## [5:05] MISLEADING: Seed oils are not burned as fuel in the body but are stored and accumulate in it.

Linoleic acid from seed oils is indeed stored in fat tissue, and adipose levels reflect intake, but it is also oxidized for energy (one review says roughly 60% goes through beta-oxidation), so the claim that it is not burned as fuel is false. The video's framing would leave viewers thinking seed oils are never used by the body, which the sources do not support.

-- [Increase in Adipose Tissue Linoleic Acid of US Adults in the Last Half Century (Advances in Nutrition)](https://advances.nutrition.org/article/S2161-8313(23)00114-X/pdf): Adipose tissue linoleic acid concentration reflects dietary intake and is strongly correlated with per-capita LA intake, supporting that LA accumulates in fat stores.

+- [Increase in Adipose Tissue Linoleic Acid of US Adults in the Last Half Century (Advances in Nutrition)](<https://advances.nutrition.org/article/S2161-8313(23)00114-X/pdf>): Adipose tissue linoleic acid concentration reflects dietary intake and is strongly correlated with per-capita LA intake, supporting that LA accumulates in fat stores.

- [Whole body oxidation of dietary fatty acids: implications for energy utilization (American Journal of Clinical Nutrition)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0002916523350172): Dietary linoleate is measured as being oxidized in the whole body, and linoleate and alpha-linolenate are described as more rapidly beta-oxidized than other fatty acids.

- [Linoleic acid: structure, synthesis, metabolites, function, foods](https://www.tuscany-diet.net/lipids/fatty-acids/linoleic-acid/): Linoleic acid is abundant in adipose tissue where its concentration reflects dietary intake, and almost 60 percent of it is oxidized by the beta-oxidation pathway.

- [Linoleic Acid in Food and Nutraceuticals](https://periodical.knowde.com/linoleic-acid-in-food-and-nutraceuticals/): Linoleic acid, like other fats, can be stored in adipose tissue as triglycerides and later mobilized and used for energy, such as during fasting or exercise.
## [5:36] UNVERIFIED: Among cooking oils, soybean oil produces the most peroxidation, followed by corn, sunflower and canola, with olive oil, beef tallow and coconut oil producing less.

- [Oxidative stability of olive, corn and soybean oil under different conditions](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0308814604001104): Oxidation indicators increased in the order soybean > corn > olive, with deep-frying causing the fastest deterioration.

- [Vegetable oil oxidation: Mechanisms, impacts on quality, and approaches to enhance shelf life](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12146556/): A 2021 frying study reported that oils high in unsaturated fatty acids (canola, soybean, sunflower) were more susceptible to oxidation than palm olein.
## [3:32] SUPPORTED: Fatty acids from seed oils get incorporated into and replace components of cell membranes.

- [Dietary linoleic acid modulates liver plasma membrane unsaturated fatty acid composition, phosphatidylcholine and cholesterol content, as well as glucagon stimulated adenylate cyclase activity - ScienceDirect](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0271531785801433): Increasing dietary linoleic acid increased linoleic acid content of liver plasma membrane phosphatidylcholine in the study.

- [Linoleic Acid - an overview](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/pharmacology-toxicology-and-pharmaceutical-science/linoleic-acid): States that the type of fatty acids predominating in a cell membrane is influenced by the fatty acid composition of the diet.
